kcet|Chemistry|2005|56||0|0.s:
Two tests, and they must be read together.
**Decolourises KMnO₄** (Baeyer's reagent) — the gas is **unsaturated**. That rules out ethane
(1) and methane (2), both saturated alkanes which leave the purple colour unchanged.
**No precipitate with ammoniacal cuprous chloride** — this reagent precipitates a red copper
acetylide, but only from a **terminal alkyne**, which has an acidic ≡C–H:
HC≡CH + 2[Cu(NH₃)₂]⁺ ⇒ Cu–C≡C–Cu↓ + 2NH₄⁺ + 2NH₃
Acetylene (4) would therefore give a precipitate, so it is excluded.
Ethene is unsaturated, so it passes the first test, but it has a C=C rather than a C≡C and no
acidic hydrogen at all, so it gives no precipitate ✓
The acidity arises because the sp carbon of an alkyne holds its electrons far more tightly than
the sp² carbon of an alkene.
∴ ethene.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|1||0|0:
Work backwards from the drug.
The **antipyretic** made by treating something with acetic anhydride is **acetanilide**,
C₆H₅NHCOCH₃, and that comes from acetylating **aniline**:
C₆H₅NH₂ + (CH₃CO)₂O ⇒ C₆H₅NHCOCH₃ + CH₃COOH
So the oily liquid is aniline.
Aniline is produced from an amide by the **Hoffmann bromamide degradation**, which removes
one carbon:
C₆H₅CONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH ⇒ C₆H₅NH₂ + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O
The starting amide must therefore be **benzamide** ✓
Check the alternatives: acetamide (1) would give methylamine, a gas, not an oily liquid;
nitrobenzene (2) is not an amide and does not undergo this reaction; aniline (3) is the
intermediate, not the starting material.
The Hoffmann reaction needs an unsubstituted –CONH₂, which benzamide has.
∴ benzamide.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|2||0|0:
The silver salt of a fatty acid is RCOOAg. Its carboxylate oxygen is nucleophilic, and the
silver ion assists the reaction by pulling the halide away from the alkyl halide:
RCOOAg + R′X ⇒ RCOOR′ + AgX↓
The product RCOOR′ is an **ester** ✓
Two things drive this. The carboxylate is a good nucleophile, and the precipitation of the
insoluble silver halide pulls the equilibrium completely to the right.
This is a useful laboratory route to esters where direct esterification is inconvenient, since
it is irreversible.
An ether (1) would need an alkoxide, RO⁻Na⁺, with an alkyl halide — the Williamson synthesis.
An amine (2) would need a nitrogen nucleophile, and an acid (3) is the starting material, not
the product.
∴ an ester.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|3||0|0:
Sort the four by what they **are**, not what they act on.
Ptyalin — the enzyme in saliva that begins the digestion of starch.
Lipase — the enzyme that hydrolyses fats.
Pepsin — the enzyme in the stomach that digests proteins.
All three are **enzymes**, which are globular proteins acting as biological catalysts.
**Cellulose** is not an enzyme at all. It is a **polysaccharide**, a structural carbohydrate made
of β-glucose units joined by β-1,4-glycosidic links — the main component of plant cell walls.
So it belongs to a different class of biomolecule entirely.
The trap is that cellulose is associated with digestion in the same breath as the enzymes —
but as a substrate (and in humans, an indigestible one, since we lack cellulase), not as a catalyst.
∴ cellulose.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|4||0|0:
Order is determined by experiment, so check each claim against the known kinetics.
(1) Decomposition of H₂O₂ — first order ✓ Correct; rate = k[H₂O₂], and the half-life is
independent of concentration.
(3) Saponification of ethyl acetate — second order ✓ Correct; rate = k[ester][OH⁻], first
order in each, so second order overall.
(2) H₂ + Br₂ ⇒ 2HBr — described as **zero order**, which is wrong ✗
This is a chain reaction with a complicated experimental rate law:
rate = k[H₂][Br₂]^½ / (1 + k′[HBr]/[Br₂])
It is roughly 1.5 order at the start, and it certainly is not zero order — a zero order reaction
would proceed at a constant rate whatever the concentrations, which is plainly not the case here.
The standard zero order examples are quite different: photochemical reactions, and reactions
on a saturated catalyst surface.
∴ statement (2) is wrongly matched.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|6||0|0.s:
A **p subshell** has three orbitals (m = −1, 0, +1), and by Pauli's principle each orbital holds
at most two electrons, which must have opposite spins.
So a filled 2p subshell contains 6 electrons:
3 orbitals × 2 electrons = 6
Of those six, exactly **half** have s = +½ and half have s = −½, because the two electrons
sharing any one orbital must be paired.
number with s = −½ = 6/2 = **3**
That is the maximum the 2p subshell can hold with that spin, and it is what the question asks
for.
Option (3), 6, is the total number of 2p electrons regardless of spin, and option (1), 2, is the
capacity of a single orbital.
∴ 3.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|7||0|0.s:
Work out the molecular formula of each and look for the odd one.
2-Methylbutane — a four-carbon chain with one methyl branch: 5 carbons ⇒ **C₅H₁₂**
2,2-Dimethylpropane — a three-carbon chain with two methyls: 5 carbons ⇒ **C₅H₁₂**
Pentane — a straight chain of five: ⇒ **C₅H₁₂**
2,2-Dimethylbutane — a four-carbon chain with two methyls: 4 + 2 = 6 carbons ⇒ **C₆H₁₄**
Three of them share the formula C₅H₁₂, so those three are **chain isomers** of one another —
indeed they are the only three isomers of pentane.
2,2-Dimethylbutane has six carbons and belongs to the hexane family instead, so it is the one
that differs.
Check with CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: for n = 5, 2(5) + 2 = 12 ✓ and for n = 6, 2(6) + 2 = 14 ✓
∴ 2,2-dimethylbutane.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|8||0|0.s:
Convert the masses to moles, then set out the changes.
N₂ : 56/28 = 2 mol
H₂ : 8/2 = 4 mol
NH₃ at equilibrium : 34/17 = 2 mol
The reaction is N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, so from the 2 mol of ammonia formed:
N₂ consumed = 2/2 = 1 mol
H₂ consumed = (3/2) × 2 = 3 mol
Equilibrium amounts:
N₂ = 2 − 1 = **1 mol**
H₂ = 4 − 3 = **1 mol**
NH₃ = **2 mol**
Check by conservation of atoms: nitrogen 2(1) + 2 = 4 ✓, hydrogen 2(1) + 3(2) = 8 ✓ — the
same as the 4 mol of H₂ started with.
∴ 1, 1, 2.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|9||0|0.s:
At constant temperature and pressure the criterion for a system at equilibrium — or for a
reversible process — is
ΔG = 0
Substituting into the definition of free energy:
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
0 = ΔH − TΔS
**ΔH = TΔS** ✓
The other options are not generally true:
(1) ΔH = 0 would mean no heat change at all, which is false for a phase change or a reaction.
(2) ΔS = 0 would mean no entropy change, again false in general.
(3) ΔH = ΔE only when Δn(gas) = 0, since ΔH = ΔE + Δn(g)RT.
This relation is how entropies of fusion and vaporisation are obtained: ΔS = ΔH/T at the
transition temperature, where the two phases are in equilibrium.
∴ ΔH = TΔS.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|10||0|0:
The definitions settle it.
The **anode** is where **oxidation** occurs, so it is where electrons are released:
Zn ⇒ Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻
Those electrons cannot travel through the solution — an electrolyte conducts by the movement
of **ions**, not free electrons. They must take the wire.
So the electrons leave the anode, pass through the **external circuit** doing electrical work,
and arrive at the cathode, where they are taken up in a reduction:
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇒ Cu
Inside the cell the circuit is completed by ions moving through the solution and the salt
bridge — anions towards the anode, cations towards the cathode.
So (3) and (4) are wrong because electrons never travel through the solution, and (2) reverses
the direction.
Note that in a galvanic cell the anode is the **negative** terminal, the opposite of an
electrolytic cell.
∴ from anode to cathode through the external circuit.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|11||0|0.s:
This is a **Wurtz** reaction, which joins the two carbons that carried the halogens. With a
mixture of two different halides, the cross-coupled product is the one asked about.
The product is 2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₂CH–CH₃.
Split it at the new bond. The two fragments are:
(CH₃)₂CH–  (an isopropyl group, 3 carbons)
–CH₃    (a methyl group, 1 carbon)
Put the chlorines back where the bond was formed:
(CH₃)₂CHCl = **2-chloropropane**
CH₃Cl = **chloromethane**
Check the carbon count: 3 + 1 = 4, and 2-methylpropane is C₄H₁₀ ✓
Option (1) would give ethane and propane, (2) would give butane (a straight chain, not
branched), and (4) would give 2-methylbutane with five carbons.
The branching is the clue: a branched product needs a **secondary** halide as one partner.
∴ 2-chloropropane and chloromethane.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|12||0|0.s:
Find the false statement.
(1) True — benzyl chloride is a lachrymatory (tear-producing) liquid, and Beilstein's test
(green flame on a copper wire) detects the halogen ✓
(2) True — with alcoholic AgNO₃ it gives a white precipitate of AgCl, and it does so readily ✓
(4) True — the –CH₂Cl group is oxidised to –CHO by boiling with copper nitrate or lead
nitrate, giving benzaldehyde ✓
(3) **False** — benzyl chloride is **more** reactive than an ordinary alkyl halide, not less.
The reason is the benzene ring. Ionisation gives the benzyl carbocation, C₆H₅CH₂⁺, in which
the positive charge is delocalised into the ring over three further positions. That resonance
stabilisation makes the carbocation form far more easily, so SN1 substitution is fast.
It is this very reactivity that statements (2) and (4) are describing — which is the internal
clue that (3) contradicts them.
∴ statement (3) is incorrect.
